articles.title: Your walking speed may hold a clue to how long you’ll live, study suggests
articles.summary: A JAMA Network Open study of over 4,000 older adults found faster walking pace was linked to lower death risk over nearly 12 years of follow-up.
articles.body: The speed a person normally walks could offer a simple clue about their overall health and longevity, new research suggests. A study published in JAMA Network Open followed 4,067 adults in the U.K., who were about 69 years old on average, to see whether their usual walking pace was linked to their risk of death over time. Participants completed a short walking test at their normal pace and also wore a wrist activity tracker for nine days to capture their walking speed during everyday life. FORGET THE GYM: A 30-SECOND TEST MAY BE ONE OF THE BEST INDICATORS OF LONGEVITY Over nearly 12 years of follow-up, faster walking in both settings was linked to a lower risk of death, even after researchers accounted for other health and lifestyle factors. A total of 739 participants died during that period. Beth Templin, a board-certified geriatric clinical specialist and CEO of HouseFit Physical Therapy & Fitness in St. Louis, said walking speed can offer a broader look at how well the body is functioning. "In physical therapy, we call walking speed the 'sixth vital sign' because it's a snapshot of how well many body systems are working together," Templin, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Changes in walking speed can therefore offer clues about a person's health, according to the doctor. "To walk briskly, you need strong legs, a healthy heart and lungs, good balance, and a brain and nervous system that can coordinate it all," she said. "When walking speed starts to slip, it's often an early warning sign that one of those systems is declining, sometimes before anything shows up on a lab test," Templin added. For older adults who want to improve their walking speed and overall fitness, simply taking more steps may not be enough. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Build the engine, not just the habit," Templin advised. "Most people try to walk more, but speed comes from strength and balance." The doctor suggested strengthening the legs with simple exercises, such as standing up from a chair without using the hands and doing heel raises while holding onto a counter. She also recommended adding short bursts of faster walking. After warming up, a person could walk briskly for one minute, slow down for two minutes and then repeat, gradually increasing the faster periods. The findings do not mean that simply walking faster will make someone live longer, experts noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "This study shows an association, not proof that walking faster by itself adds years," Templin reiterated. The participants included in the study were generally healthier than the larger group, the researchers noted. There is also no single standard method for measuring everyday walking pace with wrist activity trackers. More research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to other groups. articles.title: Women with cleft lip scarring praise advance in aesthetics
articles.summary: Two women from Wales are among the growing number of people having lip filler after cleft lip and palate surgery.
articles.body:
Two young women who have turned to dermal fillers after having cleft lip surgery say it has given them confidence after they were both left with scarring.

"Now I feel like I can just go out and talk to anyone, be more social and just be confident," Amber Dorgan, 20, from Neath, said of the treatment, which is offered by the NHS as well as by aesthetic clinics.

But experts and clinics have called for regulations to be introduced for aesthetic practitioners providing the service.

It comes as one psychology academic warned people with a cleft lip were being "deliberately targeted" by the aesthetics industry and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation".

Aesthetics treatment for people with scars involves using filler to reduce their appearance, restore symmetry, and add volume after cleft lip surgery.

Dorgan was born with a cleft lip and has faced hearing difficulties, speech difficulties and bullying at school because of her scars.

She had five operations as a child, as well as regular hospital appointments for speech and language therapy.

Now she receives free dermal filler for life through The Welsh Centre for Cleft Lip and Palate based in Morriston Hospital in Swansea, something she feels extremely fortunate to have.

Dorgan said: "I've always been insecure about how I look, going out and about, I've always had anxiety and I just get nervous.

"Now the lip fillers have made me feel confident in myself a little bit more. It's helped a lot," she said.

Dorgan believes the treatment should be available to everyone with a cleft lip "because it makes you much more confident and happy".

"Before [filler] I was really shy, I wouldn't talk to anyone, I didn't want to leave the house."

A cleft lip and palate is a condition which is present from birth when the upper lip, roof of the mouth, or both, fail to fuse properly during pregnancy.

It affects one in every 700 babies born in the UK and surgery to close the cleft is typically given when a baby is three to six months old.

A cleft lip and cleft palate can cause a number of issues, particularly in the first few months after birth before surgery is carried out.

This can include difficulty feeding, hearing problems, dental problems and speech problems.

The NHS offers lifelong care to those with the condition.

Emily Evans, 21, from Kidwelly in Carmarthenshire, is a stay-at-home mum to her two young children.

She was born with a cleft lip and underwent two surgeries, one as a baby to close her cleft, and one when she was 10 to smooth out her lips.

Growing up she always felt different, as her peers would ask questions about her scar.

"Nobody hates anything more than being different," she said.

"I would often joke I was bitten by a shark."

Evans was discharged from cleft services when she was 17. She was never offered filler treatment for her scars, but was told to keep in contact.

"When I was younger, I was seeing these people who all look perfect and the same, and I didn't," she said.

"So it sort of felt like I needed to sort of get something done."

Evans said she thought aesthetics treatments might help boost her confidence.

"I understand why people might not choose to have filler, it makes people unique, it's nice to have something that makes people different," she said.

But she added: "I think more people would choose to have it if it was a more well-known option."

Both women agree that seeing more people with a cleft lip in the public eye would help young people with the condition.

Evans discovered through social media that treatments were available and found aesthetic practitioners in England offering it to those with scars.

But she said she found a lack of practitioners in Wales.

That was until Evans discovered Summer Rose-Dorland, who runs a clinic in her hometown of Somerset and sometimes runs pop-up clinics in Wales.

After completing extra training she now works with non-profit organisation CleftInject, which help adults with scarring from cleft lip surgery find aesthetic practitioners who understand the condition.

According to Rose-Dorland, some practitioners associated with CleftInject "offer a majority of our treatments free of charge", especially for people's first treatments.

She said: "A lot of my clients struggle with their scar, I have messages from people that say that they had to stand side on in photos or when they're talking to someone because they feel like they obviously have to stand a different way."

Some people may choose an aesthetic practitioner over the NHS, she said, as they believe they will have more choice about how their lips will look after.

There are currently no regulations in the aesthetics industry, and some people believe that practitioners like Summer shouldn't be allowed to offer and administer these treatments.

Rose-Dorland, who qualified four years ago and said she had since done 20 training courses, said: "I'm a non-medic and I stand for having regulation, I generally think we need it in the aesthetics industry.

"There are some people out there that just do things that are actually quite scary, but I don't think it should be that a non-medic can't practise.

"The person I trained with trains medics, so it's not just non-medic doing these trainings. There's doctors, nurses, midwives, they are all actually doing the same training as well."

Dr Neil Brierley is a consultant cleft and plastic surgeon in the West Midlands Cleft Service.

He said it was important for people who have had a cleft lip or have loved ones with a cleft to engage with NHS teams that provide lifelong support and care.

The surgeon said they could offer an " unbiased" opinion to come to "an appropriate decision between the individual that's seeking assistance and what we feel is their best and worst options".

"What we don't want is to have people who are potentially vulnerable who are looking for maybe a quick fix or a solution to feel that they don't have an option to come back to the NHS," he said.

"And they certainly do not have to, but we are here if they need us."

Brierley said everyone was entitled to their own choice about using aesthetic practitioners, but that it was important to be aware of how to deal with any complications.

"I think it's important to inform your cleft team because it may impact any further treatment that you might need," he said.

"For example if you were wanting revisional surgery, placement of filler in certain areas would prevent certain operations from being possible afterwards."

Brierley said the lack of regulations around injectables and cleft dermal fillers was also concerning.

"I know that there are a number of organisations, various world colleges and specialist societies [which] are trying to bring in regulation in line with government but at the moment the entire field is unregulated, he said.

"There will be many excellent practitioners out there, but it will be impossible to know in advance if there is someone who isn't following best practice."

Dr Nicola Stock is an associate professor whose work focuses on the psychological impact of appearance-altering conditions such as a cleft lip.

Alongside others, she has worked on a project at the University of the West of England's Centre for Appearance Research. They have looked into the use of dermal fillers for people with a cleft, the people who provide them, what experiences and qualifications they have, and how these fillers are being marketed to the community.

Stock said research suggested adults born with a cleft still had concerns with their appearance after surgery.

The research also suggested that more people born with a cleft lip were interested in aesthetics treatments like dermal filler.

She believes the way filler is being marketed on social media is fuelling this steady increase of people seeking out treatment.

"Within the general population, dermal filler has exploded in popularity in recent years, and it's now one of the most common non-surgical cosmetic procedures used worldwide," she said.

"And we believe that this is being fuelled predominately by the aesthetics industry and predominately on social media."

Stock said she was worried that adults with a cleft lip, who have a complex medical history, were being "deliberately targeted" and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation at the hands of the aesthetics industry".

Until there are more guidelines in the sector, Stock recommended that anyone considering dermal filler should research their options and get in touch with their local NHS cleft team or contact the Cleft Lip and Palate Action charity.

If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Coca-Cola CEO says Diet Coke is back, takes on 'fridge cigarette' moniker
articles.summary: Diet Coke sales surged 6% globally as the "fridge cigarette" trend raises concerns about dopamine, artificial sweeteners and emotional dependency patterns.
articles.body: A year after Diet Coke's "fridge cigarette" nickname took hold on social media, Coca-Cola's CEO is weighing in — and he doesn't seem bothered by it. During a recent interview with Yahoo Finance, Coca-Cola CEO Henrique Braun was asked whether he liked the viral nickname. "The nickname ... the consumers call it ... the way they want to call it," Braun said. ZERO-CALORIE SWEETENERS COULD ALTER THE GENES OF LATER GENERATIONS, NEW STUDY WARNS "The most important thing to us is that we don't position Diet Coke in that way," he added. "What we do is that it's a great tasting product which connects with the consumer in a very unique way." Braun also pointed to Coca-Cola's growing use of social media and digital technology, though he did not directly link those efforts to the viral nickname. "We have been incorporating digital tech and AI into our plans and communicating with consumers," he said. He added that the company is "really excited about the prospects of growth." SOME MARRIOTT GUESTS TOUT COKE'S NEW MOVE AS ‘BEST EVER’ WHILE PEPSI LOYALISTS PUSH BACK Fox News Digital reached out to Coca-Cola for comment and more information. The company's latest earnings figures show that Diet Coke is gaining momentum. "The crisp sound, the carbonation and the cold hit all offer a quick, reliable burst of stimulation or relief." The company's latest quarterly earnings report, released Oct. 27, indicated that global sales volume for Diet Coke and Coca-Cola Light increased 6% in the third quarter of 2026, driven by growth in North America and Asia Pacific. The brands also recorded volume growth of 6% in the first quarter and 7% in the second quarter, following a year of flat global volume in 2025. OLD-SCHOOL SODA WENT FROM BEING A TOP BRAND TO NEARLY UNFINDABLE But the viral nickname has also raised questions about the habits behind Diet Coke's popularity. Jonathan Alpert, a New York City-based psychotherapist, previously told Fox News Digital that the appeal of the "fridge cigarette" trend is rooted partly in the sensory experience of drinking Diet Coke. "The crisp sound, the carbonation and the cold hit all offer a quick, reliable burst of stimulation or relief, especially during stressful or transitional moments in the day," Alpert said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Alpert described Diet Coke as a potential "emotional stand-in," but cautioned against relying on it as a coping mechanism. While opting for soda is "certainly a healthier choice than cigarettes," Alpert warned that the trend is not totally harmless. "When Diet Coke becomes a daily emotional crutch, it can reinforce dependency patterns, particularly if it is being used to manage anxiety, suppress appetite or avoid discomfort," he said. Debra Muth, a Wisconsin-based naturopathic doctor, previously expressed concerns about the potential effects of artificial sweeteners on the brain's reward system. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Your brain isn't asking for aspartame or nicotine. It's asking for dopamine," Muth told Fox News Digital. "That artificial sweetener crosses your blood-brain barrier and actually makes the neurotransmitter depletion worse. You're literally borrowing from tomorrow's brain chemistry." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ She added, "Both nicotine and Diet Coke hijack your dopamine pathways." Muth argued that replacing cigarettes with soda amounts to "trading one bad habit for another." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Instead, she recommended giving "your brain what it actually needs, such as amino acids like L-tyrosine for natural dopamine production, balanced blood sugar and real stress management that restores your brain's reward system."

articles.title: Bebê de 4 meses é lançado pela janela de carro após acidente em SC | G1

articles.summary: Criança, a mãe e o motorista foram levados se feriram e foram levados ao hospital da região.
articles.body:
Um bebê de 4 meses foi lançado para fora de um carro de aplicativo após o veículo tombar em Camboriú , no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina . O acidente na tarde de domingo (1º) também deixou feridos a mãe da criança e o motorista , segundo a Polícia Militar (PM).

A passageira relatou aos agentes que o filho estava no colo no momento da batida contra o meio-fio do canteiro central da via . Com o impacto e o tombamento, o bebê foi lançado para fora do carro pela janela e caiu no asfalto .

O Corpo de Bombeiros também atendeu a ocorrência, socorreu as três vítimas e as encaminhou ao Hospital Municipal Ruth Cardoso, em Balneário Camboriú . O bebê está estável e em observação na pediatria, informou a unidade, que não comentou o estado da mãe e do condutor.

O motorista informou aos agentes que seguia no sentido Centro quando bateu no meio-fio, provocando o tombamento. Ele fez o teste do bafômetro, que deu negativo para o consumo de álcool.

articles.body:
Francisco José dos Santos, de 51 anos — Foto: Reprodução

O subtenente da Polícia Militar do Piauí, Francisco José dos Santos , de 51 anos, morreu após sofrer um infarto fulminante por volta das 11h30 desta segunda-feira (2), em Buriti dos Lopes , no Norte do Piauí.

Francisco José foi socorrido pelos próprios colegas de farda e levado ao Hospital Estadual Dr. Mariano Lucas de Sousa. Ao chegar à unidade, ele recebeu atendimento de uma equipe médica, que tentou reanimá-lo, mas o policial não resistiu.

O subtenente integrava o 31º Batalhão da Polícia Militar. Ele ingressou na corporação em 1º de setembro de 2000 e dedicou mais de 26 anos ao serviço policial.

A morte causou comoção entre colegas de profissão e pessoas próximas. Em nota, o comandante do 31º BPM lamentou a perda e manifestou solidariedade aos familiares e amigos.

O Comandante do 31º Batalhão de Polícia Militar manifesta profunda consternação e pesar pelo falecimento deste valoroso companheiro de farda.

articles.title: Dor forte e desmaios: paciente do DF tem condição rara que causa vazamento do líquido que protege o cérebro | G1
articles.standfirst: Alexandre Ferraz recebeu diagnóstico de 'fístula liquórica' em 2021 e já passou por diversos procedimentos. Cirurgia em outro estado é esperança.
articles.summary: Alexandre Ferraz recebeu diagnóstico de 'fístula liquórica' em 2021 e já passou por diversos procedimentos. Cirurgia em outro estado é esperança.
articles.body:
Alexandre Ferraz Batista de Oliveira, de 46 anos, vive com fístula liquórica — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo pessoal

As pontadas na cabeça começaram em 2021. As dores eram leves, mas foram se tornando incapacitantes com o passar dos dias.

Alexandre Ferraz Batista de Oliveira tem 46 anos e mora no Distrito Federal, onde começou a busca por uma solução. Após muitas consultas, tomografias e exames, veio o diagnóstico: uma "fístula liquórica espontânea" , condição que causa vazamento do líquido que protege e o cérebro e a medula espinhal (veja detalhes mais abaixo).

Alexandre conta que as dores que sente na cabeça e na coluna são como "queimações", que não melhoram nem com os remédios mais fortes. Além disso, sofre com desmaios e falhas de memória.

O paciente passou por diversos procedimentos, sem sucesso. A esperança da família, agora, é uma cirurgia com um neurocirurgião de São Paulo que tem experiência com esse tipo de condição.

"Quando sinto muita dor, começo a ficar com falas desconexas, sem conseguir andar. E, do nada, perco a consciência. Antes, ficava mais de um dia dormindo e não lembrava de nada que tinha acontecido", relata Alexandre.

As dores também o impedem de fazer esforços físicos. Alexandre, que trabalhava como segurança, precisou ser aposentado por invalidez.

Com duas filhas, hoje ele vive da aposentadoria e trabalha de forma eventual, como autônomo, para complementar a renda.

"Um dia você é ativo, trabalha, pega filha no colo, brinca com ela. No outro dia, é praticamente um inválido, que precisa de ajuda para muitas coisas, inclusive pagar as contas", desabafa.

Alexandre após procedimento médico para tratar condição que causa vazamento de líquido que protege cérebro e medula — Foto: Reprodução

O neurocirurgião Fabio Simões Fernandes, do Hospital Universitário de Brasília , (HUB-UnB), explica que o cérebro e a médula encontram-se imersos em um líquido chamado de "líquor" que se assemelha muito a água.

"Existe uma membrana impermeável chamada dura-máter (como se fosse um saco) onde o cérebro e a medula ficam imersos nesses líquor. Quando há alguma região de fragilidade da dura-máter com saída de líquor, chamamos de fístula liquórica ", diz.

A fístula liquórica pode ser secundária, quando é provocada por traumas ou procedimentos cirúrgicos no sistema nervoso central, ou primária, quando ocorre de forma espontânea — como no caso de Alexandre.

Segundo o médico, as fístulas espontâneas são raras, com cerca de cinco casos para cada 100 mil habitantes.

O diagnóstico é feito com base nos sintomas e nos resultados de exames. Entre as manifestações estão dor de cabeça e vômitos, que podem se intensificar durante esforços físicos ou quando a pessoa está sentada ou em pé, com melhora ao se deitar.

"As fístulas liquóricas são alterações curáveis. As lesões ser tratadas com medicação para diminuição de produção do líquor e repouso. Nos casos de não resolução, a cirurgia é indicada para correção da membrana", explica Simões.

A ex-esposa de Alexandre, Cinthia Sobral Ribeiro, que é enfermeira, conta que ele era saudável e nunca havia tido problemas graves de saúde até começar a apresentar dores de cabeça intensas, vômitos e náuseas .

Os sintomas pioravam quando ele ficava em pé e melhoravam parcialmente quando se deitava.

"O exame de sangue dele veio normal e aparentemente ele estava por dentro normal. Só que por fora ele estava tendo muito dor, vômito e desorientação. [...] Ele sempre estava prostrado, deitado e eu sempre em busca de respostas para o que estava acontecendo, porque não era mais normal. Não era uma simples infecção intestinal, não era nada conhecido. Era alguma coisa séria que estava acontecendo", lembra.

Após passar por diferentes unidades de saúde e realizar exames, ele recebeu o diagnóstico de fístula liquórica espontânea. Mas segundo Cinthia, a localização exata do vazamento era de difícil identificação, o que tornou o tratamento mais complexo.

Nenhum dos especialistas que avaliou o caso se sentiu seguro para realizar uma cirurgia, devido à complexidade do caso e à dificuldade de localizar a fístula . De acordo com ela, havia o medo de que a intervenção pudesse agravar o estado de saúde dele, e a família foi orientada a procurar um especialista em São Paulo.

Cinthia relata que Alexandre passou por vários procedimentos menos invasivos, incluindo tentativas de fechar a fístula com o próprio sangue – mas nenhum conseguiu resolver o problema.

Alexandre e Isabela; filha faz vaquinha virtual para tentar cirurgia para o pai — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo pessoal

Alexandre fez uma avaliação médica com o neurocirurgião Roger Brock, especialista nesse tipo de procedimento, que atua no estado de São Paulo. Uma cirurgia com ele é a esperança da família de Alexandre para uma melhora mais rápida.

No entanto, os custos de uma cirurgia particular são altos. Isabela Vitória, de 19 anos, filha mais velha de Alexandre, fez uma vaquinha virtual para tentar pagar a viagem e o procedimento.

"Ele falava pouco sobre a doença para não assustar a gente. Só que aí eu comecei a entender e a perceber que não estava melhorando. Eu me assustava bastante com as quedas de consciência dele, porque às vezes eu achava ele 'dormindo' na cozinha, no banheiro", conta Isabela.

"É muito difícil ver isso todo dia, ainda mais porque eu estudo e trabalho o dia inteiro, então sempre fico pensando como eu vou achar o meu pai quando eu chegar em casa, se ele vai estar bem, se ele vai estar desmaiado. Foi por isso que eu decidi fazer logo essa vaquinha", diz a filha.

Segundo Isabela, o orçamento para a cirurgia no Hospital Sírio-Libanês, um dos hospitais onde o médico Roger Borck atua, é de R$ 71.930 , mas esse valor é apenas uma estimativa e poderá aumentar conforme a evolução do tratamento.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, ela havia arrecadado R$ 1.805 com a vaquinha.

O major da reserva do Corpo de Bombeiros Adailton Alves Pereira, de 53 anos, morreu neste domingo (1º), no Hospital Regional de Araguaína (HRA), após não resistir aos ferimentos provocados por um acidente de carro na BR-153, no sábado (31).

Conforme informações preliminares, Adailton estava em um caminhão quando sofreu o acidente. Ele também atuava como pastor na Igreja Assembleia de Deus do Aureny III, em Palmas. O major foi levado ao HRA, mas não resistiu aos ferimentos.

A igreja prestou solidariedade aos amigos e familiares. "Sua dedicação à obra de Deus será lembrada com respeito, gratidão e carinho por todos nós", diz um trecho da mensagem publicada pela instituição.

O Corpo de Bombeiros do Tocantins também manifestou solidariedade aos amigos e familiares. "Neste momento de imensa dor, expressamos nossas sinceras condolências aos familiares e amigos", diz trecho da nota da corporação.

Conforme a Igreja Assembleia de Deus do Aureny III, o cortejo fúnebre está previsto para as 15h30.

articles.title: Queda de asa-delta no Rio: instrutor e passageiro morrem em São Conrado | G1
articles.standfirst: A dupla saltou da Rampa da Pedra Bonita e teve problemas ao pousar. Equipamento acabou batendo com força no muro entre o calçadão e a areia.
articles.summary: Queda de asa-delta no Rio mata instrutor e passageiro que saltaram da Pedra Bonita e atingiram o calçadão de São Conrado; atividades no local foram suspensas.
articles.body:
Um passageiro e um instrutor morreram na queda de uma asa-delta na Praia de São Conrado, na Zona Sul do Rio de Janeiro , no fim da manhã desta segunda-feira (2). Nenhum nome havia sido divulgado até a última atualização desta reportagem.

A dupla saltou da Rampa da Pedra Bonita e teve problemas ao pousar. Segundo testemunhas, no fim da descida o equipamento fez uma curva abaixo do padrão e acabou batendo com força no muro entre o calçadão e a areia.

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado às 11h23 para o socorro. A dupla foi levada para o Hospital Municipal Miguel Couto, na Gávea, de helicóptero, em estado grave, com parada cardiorrespiratória, mas não resistiu.

Os saltos foram suspensos após o incidente.

Asa-delta caiu quase na areia de São Conrado — Foto: Reprodução

articles.title: Mulher atingida por descarga elétrica após rompimento de cabo de alta tensão em Pinheiros recebe alta da UTI | G1
articles.standfirst: Letícia Caroline dos Santos, de 33 anos, está consciente e respira sem ajuda de aparelhos, mas apresenta perda de memória recente; estado de saúde ainda é considerado grave.
articles.summary: Letícia Caroline dos Santos, de 33 anos, está consciente e respira sem ajuda de aparelhos, mas apresenta perda de memória recente; estado de saúde ainda é considerado grave.
articles.body:
Letícia Caroline dos Santos, de 33 anos, recebeu alta da Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) do Hospital das Clínicas, no Centro de São Paulo , nesta segunda-feira (2). Ela foi atingida por uma descarga elétrica após o rompimento de um cabo de alta tensão na Rua Teodoro Sampaio, em Pinheiros, na Zona Oeste da capital, na última sexta (30).

Segundo a família, Letícia está consciente e respira sem ajuda de aparelhos, mas apresenta problemas de memória recente. Ela não se lembra do acidente nem de como chegou ao hospital, por exemplo.

"Ela não se lembra de nada, não se lembra do que aconteceu, e hoje a gente percebeu que ela está com perda de memória recente. Não sabe desde quando está aqui, não sabe como veio parar aqui, não sabe de nada", afirmou Roberta Assunção, mãe da vítima.

Letícia precisou ser reanimada e chegou a ser entubada após o acidente. Apesar da evolução no quadro clínico, seu estado de saúde ainda é considerado extremamente grave, segundo a família. A equipe médica avalia os próximos procedimentos para tratar as queimaduras provocadas pela descarga elétrica.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, o acidente aconteceu por volta das 8h10, perto da estação Faria Lima, da Linha 4-Amarela do Metrô. Um médico e uma enfermeira que trabalham em um prédio em frente ao local prestaram os primeiros socorros à vítima.

Uma testemunha que trabalha com Letícia e estava logo atrás dela contou à polícia que ouviu um forte estrondo em um poste de energia, seguido de um clarão. Em seguida, um fio se desprendeu e caiu perto da mulher, que foi ao chão aparentando ter sido atingida por uma descarga elétrica.

A Enel lamentou o acidente e afirmou que apura as circunstâncias da ocorrência. A concessionária também disse que representantes mantêm contato diário com a família para acompanhar o estado de saúde da vítima e oferecer apoio, além de se colocar à disposição das autoridades para colaborar com a perícia.

O advogado da família, Márcio Santos, no entanto, contestou a informação de que a concessionária vinha prestando assistência. Segundo ele, a Enel fez o primeiro contato com a família nesta segunda, pedindo uma reunião.

Ainda de acordo com a defesa, o hospital negou o acesso e o fornecimento de informações diretamente a um representante da concessionária. Os familiares disseram que todas as informações sobre o estado de saúde da vítima seriam repassadas pela própria família.

A defesa afirmou que aguarda um posicionamento formal da empresa e cobrou uma resposta efetiva sobre o caso.

Caminhão da Enel atende ocorrência de queda de fio eletrificado na Rua Teodoro Sampaio, na Zona Oeste de SP — Foto: Henrique Silva/TV Globo

Letícia foi atingida por uma descarga elétrica na manhã de sexta-feira (30), enquanto caminhava pela Rua Teodoro Sampaio, em Pinheiros. Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, um fio de alta tensão conectado a um poste se rompeu e caiu próximo à mulher.

Uma testemunha que passava pelo local relatou à polícia ter ouvido um forte estrondo vindo do poste, seguido de um clarão. Na sequência, viu o cabo se desprender e cair no chão.

Conforme o depoimento, o fio não chegou a tocar diretamente em Letícia. No entanto, o arco elétrico provocado pela queda do cabo atingiu a mulher, que sofreu uma descarga e caiu no chão.

A vítima permaneceu consciente inicialmente e tentava respirar. Os primeiros socorros foram prestados por uma equipe de apoio de um edifício em frente ao local, formada por um médico e uma enfermeira. Depois, ela foi encaminhada ao Hospital das Clínicas.

Policiais militares foram até a unidade de saúde para identificar a vítima e colher seu depoimento, mas não conseguiram ouvi-la porque ela estava inconsciente e recebia atendimento médico.

A Polícia Civil solicitou uma perícia no local para investigar as circunstâncias do acidente.

Em nota, a Enel São Paulo lamentou "profundamente o acidente ocorrido na última sexta-feira, na Rua Teodoro Sampaio, envolvendo a rede elétrica da companhia e uma mulher de 33 anos.

Representantes da distribuidora mantêm contato diário com a família da vítima, para acompanhar seu estado de saúde e se colocar à disposição para prestar o apoio necessário. Ontem, a família indicou um advogado, que passará a intermediar o contato com a empresa.

A companhia apura as circunstâncias do acidente e permanece à disposição das autoridades competentes para colaborar com a perícia."

A assessoria jurídica da família informou que acompanha o caso e aguarda os resultados da perícia e do inquérito policial para identificar as causas do rompimento do fio e apurar eventuais responsabilidades.

A defesa também citou o artigo 37, parágrafo 6º, da Constituição Federal, que estabelece a responsabilidade objetiva das concessionárias de serviços públicos por danos causados a terceiros.

Os familiares disseram confiar nas instituições e defenderam uma investigação rigorosa, transparente e rápida. Neste momento, segundo a nota, a prioridade é a recuperação de Letícia e a preservação de sua vida.

articles.title: Ladrões atiram em vigilante da Ceagesp de Ribeirão Preto, SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima foi socorrida e foi encaminhada para a Unidade de Emergência do Hospital das Clínicas (HC-UE), onde passou por cirurgia.
articles.summary: Vítima foi socorrida e foi encaminhada para a Unidade de Emergência do Hospital das Clínicas (HC-UE), onde passou por cirurgia.
articles.body:
Ceagesp em Ribeirão Preto, SP — Foto: Valdinei Malaguti/EPTV

Um vigilante da Ceagesp de Ribeirão Preto (SP) foi baleado na noite de domingo (1º) e teve a arma, um revólver calibre 38, levada pelos suspeitos.

A vítima fazia a ronda noturna na área, quando foi abordada por dois criminosos encapuzados. Eles entraram em luta corporal para roubar a arma do vigilante e, em seguida, atiraram nele.

Os suspeitos fugiram do local após o crime e, até a última atualização desta reportagem, não tinham sido identificados e nem presos.

O Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) foi acionado e a vítima foi socorrida e encaminhada para a Unidade de Emergência do Hospital das Clínicas (HC-UE).

O vigilante passou por cirurgia e o quadro de saúde dele é estável. A Polícia Civil vai investigar o caso.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Ceagesp, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

O corpo do homem que estava desaparecido após submergir em uma lagoa no Povoado Aldeias, em Santo Amaro das Brotas, foi localizado no final da manhã desta segunda-feira (2). As buscas foram realizadas pela equipe de mergulho do Corpo de Bombeiros.

articles.title: Homem é baleado no bairro Surubi Velho, em Resende | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima foi atingida em uma das pernas e permaneceu internada no Hospital de Emergência; autores dos disparos não foram identificados.
articles.summary: Vítima foi atingida em uma das pernas e permaneceu internada no Hospital de Emergência; autores dos disparos não foram identificados.
articles.body:
Hospital de Emergência de Resende — Foto: Divulgação/TV Rio Sul

Um homem foi baleado na madrugada desta segunda-feira (2), no bairro Surubi Velho, em Resende (RJ). Segundo o registro policial, a vítima foi surpreendida por criminosos que saíram de uma área de mata e atiraram em sua direção.

Segundo a Polícia Civil, o caso aconteceu por volta das 2h, na Rua Prefeito Geraldo Rodrigues. O homem contou à Polícia Militar que havia estacionado o carro perto da casa da mãe quando foi surpreendido pelos suspeitos. Um dos disparos atingiu uma de suas pernas.

A corporação informou ainda que a irmã da vítima o encontrou caído na grama da calçada, próximo ao posto de saúde do bairro. Ele estava consciente, mas sentia fortes dores. Ela o levou ao Hospital de Emergência de Resende, onde permaneceu internado, com previsão de passar por cirurgia.

Ainda de acordo com a Polícia Civil, a mãe da vítima estava abrindo o portão no momento do ataque, mas não conseguiu identificar os autores. A família informou desconhecer possíveis ameaças ou desavenças envolvendo o homem.

O local não possui câmeras de segurança. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, a autoria e a motivação do crime eram desconhecidas. O caso foi registrado como tentativa de homicídio.

A identidade dos envolvidos não foi divulgada pela corporação.

articles.title: Death Café Ribeirão Preto: Projeto da USP debate luto e finitude | G1
articles.standfirst: Death Café promove rodas gratuitas sobre luto, cuidados paliativos e finitude. Desde 2022, iniciativa realizou 48 encontros e registrou mais de mil participações.
articles.summary: Iniciativa promove rodas gratuitas sobre luto, cuidados paliativos e finitude. Desde 2022, já foram 48 encontros e registrou mais de mil participações.
articles.body:
Um projeto de extensão da Universidade de São Paulo (USP) reúne pessoas de diferentes idades na Biblioteca Sinhá Junqueira, no Centro de Ribeirão Preto (SP), mensalmente para conversar sobre morte, luto, cuidados paliativos e espiritualidade em saúde.

No chamado Death Café - Pausa para o café: Vamos falar sobre morte? , os participantes chegam depois de perder alguém, acompanhar uma doença grave ou perceber que não conseguem discutir o assunto com familiares e amigos. Outros procuram os encontros por medo da própria morte, curiosidade ou vontade de refletir sobre a vida.

A enfermeira aposentada Valéria de Almeida Pereira, de 67 anos, começou a frequentar o projeto depois de perder a mãe para um câncer de pulmão, em março de 2023. Dois meses depois, encontrou nas rodas de conversa uma maneira de lidar com a saudade.

"Eu descobri que, quanto mais eu falo da minha mãe, melhor eu me sinto. Não necessariamente falar só da sua passagem, desse sofrimento que foi para nós e para ela, mas falar da mulher que ela foi, da mãe que ela foi."

A iniciativa já realizou 48 encontros e registrou mais de mil participações desde maio de 2022, segundo a coordenação . As reuniões são gratuitas, não exigem inscrição e já receberam desde adolescentes até pessoas com mais de 80 anos.

Participantes do Death Café se reúnem para conversar sobre morte, luto e cuidados paliativos em Ribeirão Preto (SP). — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Para a professora Marysia Mara Rodrigues do Prado De Carlo, da Faculdade de Medicina de Ribeirão Preto da USP e uma das coordenadoras da iniciativa, as motivações são diferentes, mas muitos participantes compartilham a dificuldade de encontrar um espaço para falar sobre a morte.

Segundo ela, a espiritualidade abordada nos encontros está relacionada à busca por sentido para a vida e não, necessariamente, à religiosidade. As conversas respeitam as diferentes crenças dos participantes e não são direcionadas a nenhuma religião específica.

"O relato que esses participantes trazem muito é que eles nunca conseguem conversar sobre isso. Os amigos ou os familiares falam 'não fala sobre isso, isso é um tema fúnebre'. Ou que, se falar, vai ser pior."

'Quanto mais falo da minha mãe, melhor me sinto'

Valéria trabalhou durante 35 anos no Hospital Santa Tereza, em Ribeirão Preto. Mesmo com a experiência como profissional da saúde, ela conta que não sabia como conversar com a mãe sobre o avanço de um câncer de pulmão, os tratamentos e os desejos para o fim da vida.

A doença foi descoberta em 2017. Durante alguns anos, a mãe continuou ativa, fazendo feira, ioga, pintura e pilates. Com o avanço dos sintomas, no entanto, começou a perder autonomia.

Valéria e a irmã sabiam que a mãe desejava permanecer em casa, mas tinham dúvidas sobre como respeitar essa escolha e lidar com as decisões relacionadas ao tratamento.

"A gente tinha muitas angústias, muitas dúvidas. Não sabia como proceder, como abordar, como discutir aquilo, o que ela queria, os seus desejos em relação à situação. Foi muito pesado."

Enfermeira aposentada Valéria de Almeida Pereira ao lado da mãe, que morreu em março de 2023 após enfrentar um câncer de pulmão — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Cerca de três meses antes da morte, a família conheceu uma médica especializada em cuidados paliativos, que passou a acompanhar a paciente em casa. Além de ajudar no controle dos sintomas, a profissional conversou com ela sobre desejos e receios.

Segundo Valéria, uma das situações mais importantes ocorreu quando a médica disse diretamente à mãe sobre o que ela queria para o período que ainda teria de vida.

"A gente não conseguia conversar com a minha mãe sobre o que ela pensava, o que ela queria. E aí a médica faz essa conversa com ela. Aquilo foi de uma grandiosidade, me deu tanto conforto a minha mãe poder falar o que ela queria."

A mãe de Valéria morreu em casa, em 25 de março de 2023, acompanhada pela família. Parentes que moravam em Minas Gerais viajaram para Ribeirão Preto e estiveram presentes nos últimos dias.

"Eu tive a bênção de conseguir me despedir dela, ficar conversando com ela baixinho. Pude fazer uma despedida que me confortou muito."

Marysia explica que os cuidados paliativos não são destinados apenas a pessoas nos últimos dias de vida. O acompanhamento pode começar durante o tratamento de uma doença grave, buscando aliviar o sofrimento e melhorar a qualidade de vida do paciente e dos familiares.

"O cuidado paliativo é falar de vida com qualidade. Ter boa qualidade de vida enquanto houver vida e, principalmente, cuidar da família. Porque, para o cuidado paliativo, cuidar da família é essencial."

Depois da morte da mãe de Valéria, a médica continuou acompanhando a família e indicou algumas possibilidades para conversar sobre o luto.

Uma delas foi o Death Café. Desde então, Valéria participa de todos os encontros e viu nas conversas uma oportunidade para lembrar da mãe, compartilhar experiências e ouvir outras pessoas que enfrentaram perdas.

Ela diz que falar sobre a mãe não elimina a saudade ou o sofrimento, mas as conversas a ajudaram a encontrar uma forma de conviver com a ausência.

Em casa, Valéria mantém fotografias da mãe espalhadas pelos cômodos e conta que ainda conversa com ela diariamente, compartilhando notícias boas e ruins.

"Para mim, o luto é para sempre. Mas hoje eu sinto que ela ocupou um espaço no meu coração com mais conforto, com menos dor. Eu converso com a minha mãe todo dia. Eu choro, conto notícias ruins, notícias boas. Cada um acha a sua forma, e o Death Café fez uma diferença nesse processo meu. Fez e continua fazendo".

Valéria de Almeida Pereira encontrou no Death Café um espaço para compartilhar lembranças da mãe e conversar sobre o luto — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A estudante de terapia ocupacional Bruna Ferreira Pepe, de 25 anos, conheceu o Death Café por meio da Liga de Espiritualidade em Saúde e Cuidados Paliativos (LESCP-USP).

Atualmente no segundo ano da graduação, ela preside a liga, ajuda a organizar os encontros e participa das conversas compartilhando experiências pessoais.

Bruna conta que, antes do projeto, evitava pensar sobre a morte. Nos últimos dois anos, porém, enfrentou três perdas : dois primos, que morreram em acidentes de trânsito, e a cachorra Nina, de 14 anos.

Segundo ela, as mortes repentinas foram difíceis, porque não houve tempo para despedida. Mas o acompanhamento no Death Café fez Bruna passar pelo período com um pouco mais de conformidade e entendimento.

"É um espaço que a gente consegue trazer esse tipo de coisa sem ter aquele medo. 'Será que eu falo sobre isso? Vai ser uma conversa ruim?' É um lugar em que você se sente livre para poder falar."

Estudante Bruna Ferreira Pepe com a cachorra Nina, que morreu aos 14 anos, em março de 2026; perda também foi compartilhada nos encontros do Death Café — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Marysia explica que mortes repentinas e doenças prolongadas estão entre os assuntos mais frequentes nas rodas. Embora sejam experiências diferentes, ambas podem deixar sentimentos que as pessoas têm dificuldade de compartilhar.

"O que a gente mais percebe é que as pessoas querem falar sobre morte, nos seus mais diferentes aspectos. A morte abrupta, que geralmente é muito traumática, mas, principalmente, a morte da pessoa com doença crônica, que tem a ver com o sofrimento prolongado."

Para Bruna, participar do Death Café não significa estar preparada para perder alguém, mas as conversas fizeram com que ela passasse a refletir também sobre a vida das pessoas que morreram, e não apenas sobre a ausência que deixaram.

"Acho que a gente pensa muito mais na vida do que na morte. Conversar sobre isso, pensar sobre morte, é mais sobre a pessoa em vida. Não que seja fácil, mas você consegue pensar melhor sobre isso, tentar se consolar."

Projeto de extensão da USP promove rodas de conversa gratuitas sobre a morte na Biblioteca Sinhá Junqueira, em Ribeirão Preto (SP) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Para Marysia, um dos principais obstáculos é o fato de a morte ainda ser tratada como um tabu . A professora define o assunto como um "interdito cultural", que costuma ser evitado mesmo quando alguém enfrenta uma doença grave ou a perda de uma pessoa próxima.

Ela conta que muitos participantes chegam ao Death Café depois de tentarem conversar sobre o assunto com familiares e amigos, mas não encontrarem abertura.

"Acontece muito o relato 'olha, eu nunca falei sobre isso, eu sempre guardei comigo, porque nunca tive com quem falar'".

Valéria também encontrou dificuldades para falar sobre a morte fora do projeto. Segundo ela, familiares e amigos frequentemente evitam o assunto, seja por medo ou por não saberem como lidar.

"É difícil você ter espaços na sociedade para conversar disso. Na família, com seus amigos, as pessoas assustam. 'Eu não quero falar de morte'".

Marysia explica que a proposta do projeto está relacionada ao conceito de educação para a morte , que busca ampliar as possibilidades de reflexão sobre a finitude, o luto e as decisões relacionadas ao cuidado.

Isso não significa, ainda segundo ela, viver constantemente preocupado com a morte, mas reconhecer que o assunto faz parte da vida e pode ser discutido antes que uma situação de perda aconteça.

"A gente tem essa ideia da educação para a morte, no sentido de que todos nós possamos lidar melhor, entendendo que a morte é parte da vida. E já tivemos diversas pessoas dizendo 'comecei a repensar minha própria finitude, comecei a conversar com a minha família sobre isso'".

Durante os encontros do Death Café, participantes compartilham experiências, perdas e reflexões sobre a finitude da vida — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Os encontros no Death Café acontecem sempre no segundo sábado de cada mês, das 10h30 às 12h, na Biblioteca Sinhá Junqueira, no Centro de Ribeirão Preto. As cadeiras são organizadas em roda e não há palestras nem temas obrigatórios.

A professora e os integrantes da liga ajudam a mediar as conversas e esclarecer dúvidas, mas não oferecem aconselhamento psicológico . A intenção é permitir que os próprios participantes compartilhem experiências.

"A gente procura sempre trabalhar de uma forma que não seja triste ou fúnebre, como as pessoas pensam. A gente brinca, a gente ri, as pessoas contam histórias. Mas é claro que também choram, também trazem histórias difíceis."

O projeto começou em maio de 2022, a partir da Liga de Espiritualidade em Saúde e Cuidados Paliativos. A iniciativa segue uma proposta internacional de rodas de conversa sobre a morte , presente em dezenas de países.

A proximidade do Dia de Finados costuma fazer com que o luto e as lembranças de familiares apareçam nas conversas realizadas em novembro. Para Marysia, a data representa uma oportunidade para que as pessoas revisitem sentimentos e reflitam sobre a própria relação com a morte.

"Eu acho que são grandes oportunidades para que as pessoas possam repensar seus próprios conceitos, que possam revisitar, muitas vezes, seus sentimentos."

Desde 2022, o Death Café reúne pessoas de diferentes idades para falar sobre a morte e ouvir histórias de outros participantes — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

articles.title: New Sussex NHS clinic for severe menopause after cancer
articles.summary: Complex menopause has severe, sudden symptoms and happens due to medical interventions.
articles.body:
A woman who went into medically induced menopause immediately after breast cancer treatment has described the experience as "horrible".

Rachel Bowman from Hove was 46 when she began treatment for breast cancer four years ago, but the medication put her into complex menopause, when symptoms happen abruptly and often more severely due to medical interventions.

"I could barely move. I could barely stand up straight. It was terrible," said Bowman.

A new pilot clinic to help breast cancer patients manage complex menopause after treatment has now opened in Brighton.

Dr Renske McFarlane who leads the project at the Royal Sussex County Hospital, said that for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.

"I felt we needed to do more to support women with that aftercare," she said.

Complex menopause happens abruptly due to medical interventions like cancer treatments, making symptoms such as hot flushes, joint pain and low mood much more severe and harder to treat.

Bowman said for her, complex menopause happened overnight.

"Your body has no time to adapt and it is like night and day.

"I had an ovarian suppressant injection one day - the next day I was dealing with 20 to 30 hot flushes a day.

"The onslaught of them was unbelievable and I was so not prepared for how I would feel and how horrific it would be," she explained.

Natural menopause is a gradual, natural, biological transition where hormone levels slowly decline over several years.

Treatments such as chemotherapy, ovarian suppression and endocrine therapies can trigger an early extreme complex menopause or cause menopause-like symptoms, including hot flushes, sleep problems, joint pain, fatigue, low mood and changes to sexual health.

To better support patients, University Hospitals Sussex (UHSussex) has launched the pilot clinic within its breast service.

A specialty doctor in breast surgery, Dr McFarlane said the pilot clinic was working to improve support for patients experiencing symptoms of complex menopause.

"Nationally, we're very good at screening, diagnosing cancers, operating and providing initial treatment," she explained.

"But for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.

"I was having more and more conversations with patients about how they were feeling, the impact on their confidence at work, their relationships and family life."

Patients can be referred to the pilot clinic by their surgeon, breast care nurse, oncology team or GP and there are plans to develop the service across Sussex.

Bowman now works with the charity Menopause and Cancer to personally try and improve support for women who have had a similar experience.

"Actually being able to speak to a clinician one-on-one and have a conversation about my personal circumstances really, really helped and really made a massive difference."

articles.title: Robotic surgery: 'All-island first' could cut gynae waiting lists
articles.summary: A woman who waited in pain for years for endometriosis surgery praises high-tech bid to end delays.
articles.body:
Like thousands of women in Northern Ireland, Colleen Crothers waited decades for medical help to treat chronic endometriosis - and, now thanks to an all-island first, she's hoping her long road will be a thing of the past.

"Robotic surgery came too late for me," she said. "I hope other women won't have to wait as long."

She is talking about a new breakthrough for female patients in Northern Ireland - the da Vinci gynae robot at Belfast City Hospital.

Operated by humans, the robot's wrists can twist and turn in tight pelvic spaces and it is said to be more precise at complex surgery than a human hand because it is steadier.

Belfast's da Vinci robot is the first of its kind on the island of Ireland and one of only a few across the UK.

It has the potential to massively reduce complex gynaecological surgical waiting lists in Northern Ireland, which affect thousands of women's physical and mental health and their ability to have children.

With an average wait of about seven years for complex surgery, which involves several specialities, delayed treatment means some women require a hysterectomy, like Colleen at 41.

She has lived with chronic endometriosis all of her adult life, having first begun to experience chronic period pain aged 14.

But it took another 22 years before she was referred to gynaecology and a scan confirmed she had both adenomyosis and endometriosis.

"I missed out so much of family life due to daily pain - pain that went on for years," she said.

"I can't have children - I have had to have a hysterectomy and I'm in early menopause.

"To be told you can't have children is hard to swallow," she said.

An urgent case, Colleen missed out on a da Vinci operation by just weeks earlier this year.

She knows the robot's arrival could mean a much better outcome for girls and women coming behind her.

"This type of technology is fantastic and it's amazing that it is now here.

"If anything like that can help another woman, I'm happy she won't have to suffer like I have."

And while her surgery was conventional rather than by a robot, finally getting the treatment she needed has been a relief.

"The outcome was good - my tummy feels lighter, and compared to before I am more or less pain free."

da Vinci became part of the Belfast City Hospital's gynaecology team in May.

It cost £2.4m and was funded through charitable donations for gynaecological services within the trust.

To date it has performed 130 surgeries - 105 of them being on women with complex endometriosis - and four consultants have been trained to use the robot.

It means that complex gynaecology cases are being treated as a priority and are not being bumped when other surgical cases, including cancer cases, come in.

BBC News NI was given access to see the da Vinci in action - and, like a real-life sci-fi creation, it has multiple towering robotic arms that hover over the patient.

While humans are also in the theatre, it gives the surgeon a digital boost with incisions more precise and less invasive.

Dr Hans Nagar, a consultant gynaecological surgeon and oncologist, is one of the surgeons trained to operate da Vinci. He said women with complex endometriosis had previously been ill-served in Northern Ireland.

"They require complex surgery involving different specialists and now da Vinci lets us do that," he said.

"It will take some time to bed in but I believe it will make a big difference and there will be other robots going elsewhere in Northern Ireland.

"That encourages young staff to either stay or to return after a time in Canada, Australia, the UK and the Republic of Ireland," Nagar added.

On Monday, endometriosis services across Northern Ireland are to get a financial boost when the health minister is expected to announce an investment of £1.95m to improve services.

That includes a £700,000 investment in two regional endometriosis centres located within the Belfast City and Altnagelvin Area hospitals, which will help develop specialist services for women with complex endometriosis problems.

Each health trust will also receive £250,000 as part of a phased investment for those women with less complex symptoms.

Ahead of the announcement, Health Minister Robbie Butler said the investment marked an "important milestone in efforts to improve women's health services" in Northern Ireland.

"By strengthening specialist and local services, reducing variation and expanding access to modern treatment options, it will help ensure more women receive the care they need, when they need it," he said.

Although Colleen has had her operation, she continues to need specialist care for endometriosis.

The symptoms she lived with for years included heavy bleeding, severe cramping, pelvic pain and tissue growing and getting trapped in the wrong places.

A night in the emergency department - where she was screaming with pain - brought things to a head and her consultant advised surgery as soon as possible.

In June, she had surgery, which included a hysterectomy and a full bowel shave to try to remove endometriosis tissue which attached her womb to her bowel.

She said the pain felt like she was being stabbed in the stomach - pain that has now been relieved thanks to surgery.

Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows in other parts of the body, most commonly around the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and pelvis.

The problem with endometriosis tissue is that it behaves exactly like the womb lining but it is trapped in the wrong place.

Lauren Best, a theatre nurse, said the arrival of da Vinci and a dedicated endometriosis centre was what women in Northern Ireland needed.

"I know how important it is for women to get back on their feet as quickly as possible and I am seeing that happen as da Vinci means less scarring and quicker recovery time - that's good for patients," she said.

Nagar said he hoped all those who gave donations that led to the purchase of da Vinci could see the money had gone to good use.

"I want to say thank you to everyone who donated to all the patients, their families, including those who have lost a loved one - their donations are helping others, and we all very grateful," he said.

Four months on from surgery, Colleen is also grateful.

She is back to work, walking her dog and said she is finally getting her buzz back.

While she is having to deal with early menopause and knowing she will never be a mum, the fact she is pain free is, at present, enough.

articles.title: Doctors settle debate over drinking coffee on an empty stomach and potential health risks
articles.summary: Gastroenterologists weigh in on whether coffee on an empty stomach truly spikes cortisol levels or causes acid reflux and other GI symptoms.
articles.body: Drinking coffee on an empty stomach is a somewhat controversial practice, with claims circulating on social media that it spikes levels of the stress hormone cortisol and harms the gut, but some gastroenterologists say it's not harmful. One social media post claimed that drinking coffee on an empty stomach can damage the lining that protects the gut from stomach acid, and in a post on TikTok, a medical professional advised against drinking coffee on an empty stomach, saying that it can cause a spike in cortisol levels. Cortisol is a steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands, which are located on top of the kidneys. It helps regulate the body's response to stress, and high or low cortisol levels can affect a person's health, according to the Cleveland Clinic. THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE "Coffee doesn't seem to cause major problems when you drink it on an empty stomach. Studies haven't really shown that it causes problems [with] your cortisol or blood sugar or any other kind of metabolic issues," Dr. Asma Khapra, a gastroenterologist at GastroHealth in Fairfax, Virginia, told Fox News Digital. Cortisol naturally peaks in the morning, according to the Cleveland Clinic, so the "spike" in cortisol some people attribute to drinking coffee on an empty stomach might just be a natural process rather than a side effect of the coffee. Consuming caffeine relaxes the muscular valve between the esophagus and stomach, according to the Cleveland Clinic, which can cause stomach acid to move up into the esophagus and possibly lead to heartburn. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Both regular and decaf coffee trigger the release of stomach acid and gastrin, a hormone that regulates digestion. This occurs whether a person has eaten, but without food, various symptoms can arise, such as nausea, burning in the abdomen, or the urge to use the bathroom, New Jersey-based gastroenterologist Dr. Douglas Weine told Everyday Health. Caffeine is a stimulant, so it can activate the central nervous system and contribute to an increase in blood pressure and heart rate, which can lead to anxiety, heart palpitations and sleep issues, Weine added. Everyone handles caffeine differently, and some are more sensitive to it than others. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ It is true that the body absorbs coffee and, therefore, caffeine more rapidly when the stomach is empty, the Cleveland Clinic says, although some people experience no negative side effects when consuming coffee on an empty stomach. According to Khapra, "it shouldn't really cause too many GI symptoms." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think it's fine if you enjoy your cup of coffee on an empty stomach," she said, with the caveat that a large amount of cream, milk, sugar or other additives is not included.

articles.title: Type 2 diabetes patients 21 times more likely to achieve remission with intensive lifestyle changes
articles.summary: A low-calorie diet paired with resistance training helped participants lose 18.5 pounds without shedding muscle, according to a new Lancet study.
articles.body: A strict routine combining a low-calorie diet with supervised strength and aerobic training helped more than half of younger adults reverse type 2 diabetes within six months, according to a study published in The Lancet Regional Health - Americas. The study, dubbed the RESET for Remission trial, found that 54% of participants under age 45 who completed the intensive lifestyle program achieved disease remission. In comparison, only 4% of participants receiving standard medical care reached the same milestone. VITAMIN SUPPLEMENT MAY DELAY DIABETES IN SELECT GROUPS, RESEARCHERS SAY Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age is historically aggressive, according to medical literature. Patients diagnosed before 45 face a faster loss of blood sugar control, earlier cardiovascular complications and a shorter overall life expectancy than those diagnosed later in life. Researchers from McGill University in Canada and the University of Leicester in the United Kingdom enrolled 96 adults between the ages of 18 and 45 who were living with obesity and early-onset type 2 diabetes. None of the participants were using insulin. The intervention group halted their blood sugar and blood pressure medications under medical supervision and began an intensive 800- to 900-calorie daily diet. SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE For the first two weeks, patients consumed only meal-replacement products. From weeks three through 12, they were allowed one structured meal of lean protein and vegetables each day alongside meal replacements, before shifting into a weight maintenance phase for the final 12 weeks. The program paired calorie restriction with supervised aerobic and resistance training twice weekly, plus one weekly solo workout. "Our study shows that it is possible to combine a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise in young adults with type 2 diabetes," lead author Dr. Kaberi Dasgupta, a professor of medicine and director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University, told Fox News Digital. "There has previously been some concern about combining the two as being too much of a burden for people. However, people in our study stayed in our study." "Our study shows that it is possible to combine a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise in young adults with type 2 diabetes." Only 10% of participants failed to complete the final evaluations, and patients attended a median of 17 out of 20 scheduled supervised gym sessions. The researchers emphasized resistance training to combat the loss of lean muscle mass, a major risk associated with rapid weight loss. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS People who lose weight through crash dieting or appetite-suppressing medications may shed muscle along with fat, experts warn. If the weight returns, some research suggests it may come back disproportionately as body fat, potentially affecting muscle health and metabolism over time. "In our study, we think the diet provoked the weight loss, and exercise helped make sure it was [not] from muscle," Dasgupta said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "We were happy and surprised that not only did people lose fat from their organs and liver, our MRI studies indicated their muscle did not decrease at all and their handgrip strength went up." Participants shed an average of 18.5 pounds over 24 weeks, while significantly boosting their treadmill endurance and overall cardiovascular fitness. To meet the official standard for remission, patients had to maintain an HbA1c blood sugar level below 6.5% after going at least 12 weeks without any glucose-lowering drugs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES After accounting for baseline health factors, researchers concluded that patients on the diet and exercise program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving routine care. Study limitations Despite the promising outcomes, experts emphasized notable limitations. The trial was small, examining fewer than 100 individuals across medical centers in England and Canada over a relatively short six-month window. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Dasgupta also noted that the study could not determine exactly what was responsible for each benefit. "The main limitation is that we had to compare the diet plus exercise with usual care," he told Fox News Digital. "We would have liked to compare diet alone against diet and exercise to perfectly prove the point that the improvements in muscle and fitness were from the exercise." The strict routine also took a physical toll. Roughly 86% of the intervention group reported mild to moderate side effects, primarily during the early weeks, including headaches, fatigue, dizziness and constipation, though researchers noted that no severe medical complications occurred. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Health professionals cautioned that diabetes remission is not a permanent cure, and sustaining an 800-calorie threshold alongside supervised gym can present steep hurdles for busy adults outside a clinical setting. Study authors noted that longer-term trials in real-world settings are still needed to determine whether patients can keep the weight off, preserve their muscle gains and remain medication-free once regular daily routines resume.

articles.title: At 58, I Had Early Signs of Alzheimer’s in My Brain. These Interventions Got Rid of Them
articles.summary: In the months leading up to my mother’s 75th birthday in June 2019, I was planning a surprise party.
articles.body: In the months leading up to my mother’s 75th birthday in June 2019, I was planning a surprise party. As I was surreptitiously making calls to her closest friends, two of them asked me with a bit of hesitation if I had noticed changes in my mother’s memory. The truth was I had — and so had my mother. She had been talking about it for a while, writing to me in an email around that time, “I know that my memory isn’t as good as it was and I repeat myself. It concerns me but I really don’t know what to do about it.” She was afraid of handing over her finances to her wonderful husband and losing control of her life in other ways. But as expected, my sweet mother told me, “Don’t worry about me, but continue to monitor what you see as a concern.” My mom has always been my role model, an example of what the next stage in life should look like. It never dawned on me that she would develop Alzheimer’s disease. She was still healthy when we first started noticing the signs. But one day, I started to lose her, a little bit at a time. Understanding My Own Alzheimer’s Risk As I began to study Alzheimer’s, I learned that having a parent with the neurodegenerative disorder increases your risk. My case was no exception. Testing revealed my mother carried two copies of a gene called APOE4. Everyone inherits one APOE gene from each parent, and the typical variations are APOE2, believed to reduce Alzheimer’s risk; APOE3, the most common, with a neutral effect on Alzheimer’s risk; and APOE 4, which increases risk. A person with two copies of APOE4 is 8-12 times more likely to develop Alzheimer’s, according to the Mayo clinic. So in October 2024, I got tested with a cheek swab I sent back in the mail. I had an APOE4 and APOE3 gene, making me two to three times more likely to develop Alzheimer’s. I was a bit relieved. As I did more research, I learned about the work of Lisa Mosconi, Ph.D., director of the Alzheimer’s Prevention Program at Weill Cornell Medicine. A June 2020 study of hers found that hormonal shifts in menopause can increase the risk of Alzheimer’s — women make up two-thirds of cases — and that changes in the brain can start years or possibly decades before symptoms appear. In April 2025, I decided to apply to join one of her studies. I qualified, but the waiting list was a year and a half. The following month, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the first-ever blood test to help diagnose Alzheimer’s. It crossed my mind that the timing was a gift from God. “The test measures certain proteins, including a specific form of the tau protein, that can indicate the presence of amyloid plaques in the brain. An amyloid plaque is a buildup of protein that is considered the hallmark sign of Alzheimer’s disease,” the Mayo Clinic explains. I got it as soon as I could, and my results were way out of the normal range. I’d thought I was too young and that my occasional forgetfulness with words was due to menopause brain fog. My job as a news producer is active, always running, pushing, managing. It’s demanding, but I love it. I wondered if I’d have to quit and started contemplating memory care facilities where I could live and have someone take care of me. Taking Control of My Health Then, a physician friend recommended I go to the Alzheimer’s Prevention Clinic in New York City. I was told the clinic’s wait list was a year and a half and sent an email pleading them to consider me. Three days later, my phone rang. At 58, I had my first appointment with Dr. Sonja Blum, which included body composition metrics, blood and genetic biomarker panels, standardized cognitive tests and neurological exams. Afterward, I was handed customized guidelines for diet, exercise, supplements, sleep and more. Research estimates that up to 45% of dementia cases could be delayed or prevented by targeting modifiable risk factors like obesity, high cholesterol and social isolation. So, I saw my new lifestyle as a life-and-death situation with the outcome in my hands. I already had a relatively healthy diet and worked out regularly, but I needed to be doing more. I cut out artificial sweeteners and limited fried and processed foods, red meat, cheese, sweets and alcohol. Every day, I started eating leafy greens, whole grains, veggies and fruit, and every week multiple servings of fish, walnuts, almonds, avocado and berries. I also intensified my workouts to 45-60 minutes of cardio three to four days a week, plus strength training — three muscle groups, three sets per exercise, 8-10 reps. I moved up my bedtime, too. And in December 2025, I added something else: an anti-amyloid infusion, called Kisunla, approved by the FDA in 2024. A previous scan of my brain had found I had elevated levels of amyloid in every quadrant, and Kisunla has been shown in trials to slow cognitive and functional decline by 60% in patients like me. The sooner a patient starts, the more effective it is. I couldn’t wait to get the amyloid off my brain. After six infusions, in May this year, I had another scan to determine my progress. I went from a score of 86 to a 4. The radiologist wrote in the notes, “The amyloid issue has resolved.” The following month, I joined another research initiative, led by Dr. Richard Isaacson, the founder of the Alzheimer’s Prevention Clinic, who’s since moved to Florida. His team’s blood tests showed that my tau levels were normal, possibly from watching what I eat. He called the change in my amyloid levels “jaw-dropping.” A New Generation of Alzheimer’s From the moment I stepped into the Alzheimer’s Prevention Clinic, I was told, “You are the patient we want to come through our door,” a reference to my age, high level of functioning and total commitment to doing whatever I can. I currently don’t have Alzheimer’s or even mild cognitive impairment. But I still do have positive biomarkers and an elevated risk for the disease. If I were giving advice to others, there are a few things I believe are crucial to my story. My determination was not to be outmatched by my discipline. It was tough to find the right doctors and get an appointment, but I didn’t take no for an answer. Information is power. To stick my head in the sand and wait until I saw signs like those my mother exhibited would’ve been too late. We were able to slow down or even stop the progression of my symptoms years before they got worse. Blum told me that I’m the beginning of a new, groundbreaking generation of Alzheimer’s disease, one where it’s managed like any other chronic condition. That said, my journey isn’t over. There is no certainty, and I’m still a patient at the Alzheimer’s Prevention Clinic, where my blood and biomarkers are checked monthly. My mother would be proud. At 82, she still recognizes and loves me as much as ever, but she no longer can follow or remember our conversations. I have lost my closest confidant. She remains my example of how to live and grow. In trying to save my beautiful mother, I believe God helped me save myself, and I hope my story will help others until we are no longer talking about this disease anymore.

articles.title: Dietitian Shares Her Favorite High-Protein Food to Balance Blood Sugar
articles.summary: You can use food to manage blood sugar spikes and keep your energy steady throughout the day. A dietitian recommends one high-protein and high-fiber food to help.
articles.body: You don’t have to accept the rollercoaster of blood sugar fluctuations. If you’re strategic about what you eat, you can keep your energy levels stable throughout the day. With the right combination of nutrients, your body will digest food more slowly, leading to more stable blood sugar levels and better sustained energy as a result, TODAY.com explained previously. And there’s one healthy plant protein food that will help you hit all the nutritional boxes to manage blood sugar spikes. Nutrition Tip of the Day: Eat More of This Food to Get Blood Sugar Balancing Fiber and Protein When stable blood sugar is your priority, try lentils, says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. “They have a really impressive combination of protein and fiber,” she told TODAY.com previously. In just a half-cup serving of lentils, you’ll find about 9 grams of protein and 8 grams of fiber. Why It Matters “Protein, fiber and healthy fats are the three nutrients that contribute to balanced blood sugar,” Rizzo said previously. “Fiber slows digestion and the absorption of carbohydrates, while protein and fat also help make a meal more satisfying and slow the rise in blood sugar.” That’s one reason why plant-based proteins are so helpful: “They do double duty,” Rizzo noted. While foods like beans, chickpeas and lentils pack both protein and fiber, nuts and seeds provide protein and healthy fats (and, often, some fiber too). How to Get Started Lentils are a versatile ingredient that naturally work well in soups and stews. But you can also add them to salads, mix them into dips and throw them in with sheet-pan vegetables. Here are a few recipes to get you started: Lentil HummusTahini Lentils With Crispy Spiced GarlicSheet-Pan Gnocchi With Vegetables, Lentils and LadolemonoWarm Lentil SaladLentil Tacos And don’t forget about the full rainbow of lentil varieties: Choose from green, red, brown and even black lentils to suit each dish you’re making and to keep your meals exciting. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Channel 4 documentary and journalists 'poisoned the well' against Russell Brand, court hears
articles.summary: Brand's defence barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".
articles.body:
Journalists "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting complainants to come forward and make criminal allegations against Russell Brand, jurors have heard.

In his closing speech on Monday, Ian Winter KC, Brand's defence barrister, said a Channel 4 documentary and stories in the Times and Sunday Times that made allegations about Brand in 2023 "caused people who had not previously considered for it to be appropriate to bring criminal allegations against him, to do so, and very many years after."

Brand faces seven counts; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

On Monday at Southwark Crown Court, Winter told jurors that "living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful".

He added: "Can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand, that he raped just three of them?"

Winter said it was an "extremely curious feature" of the case that Brand "obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that's the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal".

He added that there was "no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it's normal".

Referring to one allegation from 1999, Winter said: "You would have to be a psychopath" to be raping someone and "asking if they were enjoying it" at the same time.

"He left her his actual email address. Rapists do not give out their email address," he added.

"Rapists do not leave their photographs. Rapists do not kiss their victims goodbye."

Referring to the Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, which made allegations about Brand in 2023, Winter reminded jurors that the judge in the trial had directed them that the programme was "very one-sided" and "produced in a dramatic manner".

The barrister said it was "published without a single journalist ever speaking to Mr Brand about it other than to protect their defamation risk... protect their right to reply after the programme had been made".

He later said: "Most importantly, that programme and those allegations in it - Mr Brand is innocent of them.

"So, they poisoned the well in respect of things of which Mr Brand is innocent."

He added that the six complainants in the case were "not random", adding they were "thoroughly contaminated by the programme".

Jurors were reminded about what Brand had said in his evidence about the impact the programme had on him.

Winter said one "graphic" example of the "truly devastating effect" on Brand was when a hospital "would not permit him to visit the bedside of his baby son after life-saving open heart surgery".

Winter said: "That tells you the extent to which public opinion has... corrupted."

Brand previously told jurors that Great Ormond Street Hospital didn't let him stay with his son due to "material that had been published in the public eye".

Brand's lawyer also told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

"Disgusting, distasteful, immoral, who cares?" he added.

"It's irrelevant to your consideration."

Winter added he was "Sorry to have to say it's not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex," nor is it "criminal to be disrespectful, or be rude, or to behave like a crazy idiot."

Winter also referred to evidence given by Brand's wife Laura, saying: "She fell in love with that man in full knowledge of what he was doing.

"She married him, she bore him three children."

He went on to say that she would not have done so if Brand was "guilty as charged".

Brand arrived at court today accompanied by his wife Laura and her father Bernard Gallacher, the former professional golfer.
