articles.title: Christa Pike's execution doctor says misplaced IV sent lethal drugs into her arms instead of veins
articles.summary: Dr. Mark Fowler reveals an improperly placed IV sent pentobarbital into Christa Pike's tissue instead of her bloodstream during the failed execution.
articles.body: The doctor who participated in Christa Pike's failed execution in Tennessee says an improperly placed IV sent lethal drugs into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream — and acknowledged the execution team should have stopped when the death row inmate complained of pain. Dr. Mark Fowler, who served as the physician during Pike's Sept. 30 execution attempt, offered a rare firsthand account of what went wrong in an interview with New York Magazine published Friday. Pike, 50, survived after receiving two doses of pentobarbital and was hospitalized for days before eventually regaining consciousness. TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT The doctor told the magazine he knew something was wrong when Pike's execution stretched to about 45 minutes. When he was called into the chamber, she was still alive and gasping for air. Fowler said he initially considered whether Pike's response to the medication could simply be taking longer than expected and decided to give it more time. DEATH ROW INMATE UNCONSCIOUS ON VENTILATOR AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION FOR TEEN’S KILLING: ATTORNEYS As another half-hour passed, he became concerned that Pike could survive with irreversible brain damage. Fowler later diagnosed her as comatose before a deputy commissioner ordered the execution stopped. He then ordered oxygen, and Pike was taken by ambulance to Vanderbilt University Medical Center. 911 OPERATORS QUESTIONED WHETHER CHRISTA PIKE FAILED EXECUTION CALL WAS PRANK, AUDIO REVEALS Fowler told New York Magazine that the IV used to administer the pentobarbital had not been properly inserted into Pike's veins. "It was delivering medicine to the subcutaneous tissue" of her arms, Fowler said. DEATH ROW KILLER CHRISTA PIKE DESCRIBES WAKING UP AFTER EXECUTION SHE NEVER EXPECTED TO SURVIVE Pike's attorneys previously said in a court filing that she complained of severe arm pain during the execution, telling those in the chamber, "My arm feels like it’s about to burst open." "They should have stopped and reassessed, and they didn’t," Fowler told New York Magazine. CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEY SAYS SHE'S 'UP AND WALKING' MORE THAN A WEEK AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION The account comes days after Pike described the aftermath of the failed execution in a statement released by her attorneys, saying she remains in constant pain and still struggles to speak. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts," Pike said Friday. "I still struggle to speak." Pike also said she was "deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position." Fowler's role in Pike's failed execution was not his first to draw scrutiny. CHRISTA PIKE EXECUTION FAILURE SPARES MURDERER WHO BAILED VICTIM OUT JUST TO KILL HIM New York Magazine reported that Fowler was also involved in the 2025 execution of Byron Black and the failed May execution of Tony Carruthers. In the Carruthers case, Fowler attempted to place an IV near Carruthers' clavicle after paramedics were unable to establish traditional IV access. Fowler told the magazine he ultimately stopped because he lacked adequate anesthetic and the procedure was becoming too painful for Carruthers. Still, Fowler said Tennessee's lethal-injection protocol needs to change. He called for fewer handoffs among execution team members and said those responsible for placing IV lines should remain in position to monitor them as the lethal drugs are administered. articles.title: New cancer treatment approach could help immune cells fight tumors longer
articles.summary: UCLA researchers found that boosting p53 protein with navtemadlin helped T cells fight melanoma cancer cells longer, but dosing challenges remain.
articles.body: Scientists may have found a way to help the body's immune cells fight cancer for longer, potentially making some treatments more effective. Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that temporarily boosting a protein called p53 helped specially prepared immune cells stay stronger and kill more melanoma cells in laboratory experiments. The study, published in Frontiers in Immunology, focused on T cells, which are immune cells that help the body fight disease. NEW CANCER VACCINE DELIVERS STUNNING RESULT AGAINST ONE OF THE DEADLIEST SKIN CANCERS Some cancer treatments take a patient's T cells, modify them in a lab so they can recognize cancer, and then return them to the body to attack tumors. One challenge is that these cells can eventually become "exhausted," making them less effective at fighting cancer, the UCLA researchers said. To address that problem, researchers treated human T cells with an experimental drug called navtemadlin, which temporarily increases the activity of p53, a protein known for helping to prevent cancer. The treated T cells showed fewer signs of exhaustion, had more energy and developed characteristics that could help them last longer. When tested against melanoma cells in the lab, they were also significantly more effective at killing the cancer cells than untreated T cells, according to the research. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Kien Vuu, a Los Angeles-based triple board-certified physician and former UCLA assistant clinical professor, confirmed that T-cell exhaustion is one of the biggest challenges encountered with these treatments. "After repeated encounters with cancer, they become 'exhausted' and lose their ability to multiply and attack," Vuu, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital. Vuu said the approach could offer a relatively simple way to strengthen existing treatments. "The practical appeal is simplicity," he said. "Rather than adding another genetic modification, this approach adds a drug during the manufacturing step, when a patient's T cells are being prepared in the lab." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER If the approach works in further research, Vuu said it could potentially help T cells remain effective for longer, particularly when treating solid tumors. The findings are still preliminary, however. "This is early, laboratory-stage research," Vuu acknowledged. "The experiments were done with human cells in a dish against melanoma cells, not in animals or people." Researchers will need to test the approach in animals and other types of cancer before moving into clinical trials, according to Vuu. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The amount of the drug will also need to be carefully studied. The UCLA researchers found that higher doses caused more T cells to die, while lower doses produced the desired effects without substantially reducing the number of healthy cells. "Dosing is especially important," Vuu said. "The researchers found that too much p53 activation actually killed more of the T cells, so getting the balance right will be critical." articles.title: Dangerous mosquito-borne virus surges in popular US state as cases reach highest levels in decades
articles.summary: Florida's dengue fever outbreak has reached 485 locally acquired cases, with Tampa Bay accounting for 95% of infections and emergency declarations issued.
articles.body: Florida health officials have confirmed 485 locally acquired cases of dengue fever this year, as the state grapples with its largest outbreak in decades. Between Oct. 18 and Oct. 24, state surveillance logged 60 new infections, with the Tampa Bay area accounting for roughly 95% of all locally acquired cases recorded statewide, according to the Florida Department of Health. The surge prompted emergency declarations in Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties in late September, allowing for faster purchasing and spraying and requests for state and federal reimbursement. Hillsborough County has since extended its state of local emergency amid ongoing transmission. DENGUE FEVER OUTBREAK TRIGGERS STATES OF EMERGENCY IN 3 SOUTHERN COUNTIES The locally acquired infections are separate from more than 300 travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year. The Florida Mosquito Control Association said mosquito abatement teams are stepping up targeted ground spraying, aerial applications and localized property inspections. What is dengue fever? Dengue is a viral illness transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. The virus can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, nausea, rash and, in severe cases, dangerous complications or death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Unlike many mosquito species that bite mostly at dawn and dusk, the mosquitoes carrying dengue feed aggressively during daytime hours and thrive in humid residential environments. DEADLY MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS CLAIMS FIRST LIFE IN MAJOR US CITY AS CASES SPREAD "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health previously told Fox News Digital. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Public health officials emphasize that Aedes mosquitoes are "container breeders," requiring as little as a tablespoon of standing water to lay eggs. Officials urge residents to inspect yards weekly and drain or cover birdbaths, gutters, planters, discarded tires and outdoor containers. Most people infected with dengue experience mild or no symptoms, typically recovering within two weeks, according to Mayo Clinic. Severe dengue can progress rapidly within 24 to 48 hours after the initial fever drops. Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, difficulty breathing, mucosal bleeding and extreme lethargy.
